cues.text: Section four covers IT service management frameworks, beginning with ITIL 4.
ITIL is guidance for managing IT-enabled services.
ITIL 4 uses a Service Value System, or SVS, which converts opportunity and demand into value.
The SVS has five components: guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, practices, and continual improvement.
Let us look closely at the service value chain.
It contains six interconnected activities: plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain or build, and deliver and support.
These activities can be combined into value streams, rather than being followed as one rigid sequence.
So an organisation might route work through different combinations of these activities, depending on what is needed.
Next, the four dimensions.
They are organisations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes.
Ignoring any one of these dimensions can undermine delivery.
Now the seven guiding principles.
First, focus on value.
Second, start where you are.
Third, progress iteratively with feedback.
Fourth, collaborate and promote visibility.
Fifth, think and work holistically.
Sixth, keep it simple and practical.
And seventh, optimise and automate.
ITIL 4 also describes 34 management practices.
And remember that value is co-created through interaction between providers and consumers.
Moving on to the second framework: ISO/IEC 20000.
ISO/IEC 20000-1 specifies requirements for a service management system, or SMS.
Organisations can obtain independent certification against those requirements.
The standard emphasises documented responsibilities, service planning, delivery, measurement, audit and improvement.
An important qualification: certification concerns the management system, not a guarantee that every service is perfect.
The third framework is the Microsoft Operations Framework, or MOF.
MOF provides practical guidance for operating IT services, and it is historically associated with Microsoft environments.
MOF 4.0 organises activities into three phases: Plan, Deliver and Operate.
These are supported by a Manage layer, which covers governance, risk, compliance, change and configuration, and team responsibilities.
Now let us compare the three frameworks using the table, row by row.
The table has three columns: the framework, its main emphasis, and a suitable application.
In the first row, ITIL 4.
Its main emphasis is value, service practices and improvement.
A suitable application is improving customer support and service delivery.
In the second row, ISO/IEC 20000-1.
Its main emphasis is auditable service management requirements.
A suitable application is independent certification and consistent controls.
In the third row, MOF.
Its main emphasis is practical operational lifecycle guidance.
A suitable application is structured infrastructure and service operations.
To close this section: these approaches can complement each other.
For example, ITIL guidance can help implement practices within an ISO 20000 service management system.
